title: Masterson v. Sine
summary: The court allowed evidence of a family agreement limiting assignment of a repurchase option because the deed was not necessarily the complete expression of the parties’ bargain.
notes:
After the 1958 conveyance Dallas Masterson went bankrupt; the plaintiffs seeking a declaration of the right to exercise the option were his bankruptcy trustee and Rebecca Masterson, and Medora Sine was Dallas's sister, so the Sines' evidence went to whether the option was personal to the Mastersons and beyond the trustee's reach.

The majority opinion (68 Cal.2d 222, 436 P.2d 561 (1968)) was written by Chief Justice Traynor.

sections.Parties: Dallas and Rebecca Masterson conveyed their ranch to Medora and Lu Sine. Medora was Dallas’s sister. After Dallas’s bankruptcy, his trustee and Rebecca sought to exercise the reserved option.
sections.Material Facts:
The 1958 grant deed reserved a ten-year option to repurchase for the original consideration plus the depreciation value of improvements. It did not state that the option was nonassignable or that the deed contained the entire agreement. The Sines offered evidence that the parties intended to keep the ranch within the Masterson family and made the option personal to the grantors.

The trial court accepted outside evidence explaining the price as $50,000 and clarifying how depreciation would be calculated, but excluded evidence of the asserted limitation on assignment. The family setting, the deed’s formal structure, and its function of giving notice to later purchasers mattered to whether that additional term would naturally have appeared in the recorded document.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the court declared the plaintiffs entitled to exercise the option and retained jurisdiction over its exercise and the price calculation. The California Supreme Court reversed because evidence concerning nonassignability had been excluded. The decision did not conclusively establish that the alleged oral limitation actually existed.
sections.Issue: Did the parol evidence rule prevent proof that a written repurchase option, silent about assignment, was intended to be personal to the grantors?
sections.Holding: No. The court held the evidence admissible because the alleged collateral agreement could naturally have been made separately from this deed.
sections.Reasoning:
The governing inquiry was whether the parties intended the writing as the exclusive embodiment of the relevant agreement. The writing supplies evidence of that intention but cannot invariably establish its own completeness. Circumstances and the subject of the alleged collateral agreement also matter.

The deed lacked an entire-agreement clause and said nothing about assignability. A recorded option could protect the grantors against later purchasers without spelling out every personal understanding among family members. The court found no indication that these parties appreciated the disadvantages of leaving the family restriction out. That made the restriction the kind of agreement that might naturally be made separately. The usual legal presumption of assignability did not itself prohibit evidence rebutting that presumed term.

The admissibility decision must be separated from proof. Allowing testimony leaves the fact finder to decide whether the family restriction was actually agreed upon. It also differs from interpreting the option’s price language, which the trial court had properly clarified through extrinsic evidence.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It illustrates partial integration, contextual evidence of completeness, and the difference between excluding a claimed term and deciding whether that term was proved.

topics.parol-evidence: The deed did not necessarily exclude a consistent collateral restriction.
topics.assent: The scope of the writing depended on what the parties intended it to embody.
topics.interpretation: Outside evidence could explain the option’s price formula.
topics.assignment: The asserted personal restriction would limit transfer of the option to the trustee.
topics.integration: The threshold question was whether the deed was a final and complete integration, and Traynor's opinion rejects the four-corners test for deciding that.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Burke, joined by Justice McComb, argued that the oral restriction contradicted an absolute written grant and its legal incident of assignability. The dissent stressed the ease of writing a nonassignment clause and the danger of using family testimony to remove an asset from bankruptcy creditors.

mnemonic.rationale: A ranch and an option the family kept
